introduction: On this Sunday, Peter declares that Jesus is the Christ, and then Jesus begins to teach that the Son of Man must suffer, be killed and rise again. Whoever wants to follow him must deny himself and take up his cross. Isaiah's servant sets his face like flint, and Saint James reminds us that faith without works is dead. Let us follow Jesus on the way of the cross.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, the Lord listens to our voice and our cry for mercy. Let us bring him our prayers.
intentions: For the Church: that she may proclaim Christ crucified and follow him faithfully, even when the way is hard. Let us pray to the Lord.
For Christians who suffer for their faith: that the Lord may help them and they may not be put to shame. Let us pray to the Lord.
For the poor who lack daily food and clothing: that Christians may show their faith by their works. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who are carrying a heavy cross: that they may know that Jesus walks with them. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may answer the question of Jesus, Who do you say that I am, with our lives. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Lord Jesus, you call us to deny ourselves and take up our cross. Give us faith that shows itself in love, and the courage to follow you to the end. You live and reign for ever and ever.

reflection.title: Who do you say that I am?
reflection.body:
This Gospel is the turning point of Mark's account. Jesus asks his disciples, "Who do men say that I am?" and then, more personally, "But who do you say that I am?" Peter answers, "You are the Christ." He is right.

But then Jesus explains what kind of Messiah he is: "the Son of Man must suffer many things, and be rejected... and be killed, and after three days rise again." Peter cannot accept it. He takes Jesus aside and rebukes him. Jesus' answer is one of the sharpest in the Gospels: "Get behind me, Satan! For you have in mind not the things of God, but the things of men." Peter has the right title but the wrong idea of what it means.

Then Jesus speaks to everyone: "Whoever wants to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me." And he gives the paradox at the heart of Christian life: "For whoever wants to save his life will lose it; and whoever will lose his life for my sake and the sake of the Good News will save it."

Isaiah's servant shows the same path: insulted and struck, he does not turn back, "For the Lord GOD will help me." And Saint James makes it practical. Faith that only says kind words to a hungry person, "Go in peace. Be warmed and filled," without helping them, is not real faith. "Even so faith, if it has no works, is dead in itself."

To say that Jesus is the Christ is not only a statement but a commitment. This week, think about the cross you are carrying, or the one you are avoiding. Ask Jesus for the grace to carry it with him. And let your faith show itself in one concrete act of help.
